slides.narration: Welcome. Glimpses of India is three short pieces about three very different regions: Goa, Coorg and Assam. In this first part, we study A Baker from Goa. Before anything else, please read the chapter itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat the text. We will understand its ideas, its picture of Goan culture, its tone, and how to answer board questions.

slides.heading: The chapter at a glance
slides.body_md: Three regions, three writers, three kinds of writing. Part 1 covers Goa, Part 2 Coorg, Part 3 Assam and a comparison of all three.

rows: short story with facts and legends

visual.caption: Glimpses of India: three regions, three kinds of writing.

slides.narration: Here is the whole chapter at a glance. A Baker from Goa is a personal memoir of childhood. Coorg is travel writing about a hill district of Karnataka. Tea from Assam is a short story that mixes dialogue, facts and legends. In exams, you may be asked about one piece, or to compare the three. Read all three in your textbook, once each, before using these slides.

a personal memoir, first person, looking back on childhood

slides.narration: A Baker from Goa is by the Goan writer Lucio Rodrigues. It is a memoir, so the writer speaks in the first person and looks back on his own childhood. Goa was ruled by Portugal for centuries, until nineteen sixty-one, and the Portuguese brought their bread with them. Learn four Goan words: pader, the baker; kabai, his old dress; bol, a sweet bread; and bolinhas, coconut cookies.

slides.heading: The piece in five stages
slides.body_md: From the Portuguese past to the writer's childhood to the baker's place in village life. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of A Baker from Goa: elders miss the Portuguese loaves; the pader still bakes; the baker's daily visits in the writer's childhood; bread for every occasion; the baker's dress, accounts and prosperity.

slides.narration: The piece moves in five stages. Older Goans miss the famous loaves of Portuguese times. Yet the pader still bakes today. The writer remembers the baker's daily visits in his childhood. He explains how bread is needed for every occasion. And finally he describes the baker's dress, his way of keeping accounts, and how well the trade paid. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: the Portuguese past and the pader today
slides.body_md: Older Goans look back fondly on the days of Portuguese rule and especially on its bread. The rulers are gone, but the bread-makers remain: traditional furnaces are still in use, the baker's bamboo staff still announces him in some villages, and sons often continue their fathers' trade. Goans still call the baker a *pader*.
slides.narration: In your own words, the piece begins with nostalgia. Older Goans remember the Portuguese days and their famous bread. The Portuguese have gone, but the bakers have not. Their furnaces are still lit, the sound of the baker's bamboo staff can still be heard in some villages, and often a son carries on his father's trade. In Goa, such a baker is still called a pader.

slides.heading: Summary 2: the baker in the writer's childhood
slides.body_md: In the writer's childhood, the baker came at least twice a day: on his morning round and on his way back with an empty basket. The children ran to meet him at the sound of his staff, not for the loaves, which the servants bought, but for bread-bangles and sweet bread. Pushed aside, they climbed up to peep into his basket. The writer jokes that children hardly bothered to clean their teeth.
slides.narration: Next, the writer remembers his childhood. The baker came at least twice a day. At the sound of his bamboo staff, the children ran out to greet him. They did not care about the loaves, which the servants bought. They wanted the bread-bangles and sweet bread. Pushed aside by the adults, they climbed up to peep into his basket. The memories are fond and funny.

slides.heading: Check: the baker's visit in order
slides.narration: Your turn. Six moments from the baker's morning visit are shuffled. Put them in the order the writer remembers them, from the first sound of the bamboo staff to the children peeping into the basket.

slides.heading: Summary 3: bread, dress, accounts and prosperity
slides.body_md: Bread is part of every celebration: *bol* for marriage gifts, sandwiches for a daughter's engagement, cakes and *bolinhas* for Christmas. So every village needs its baker's furnace. Bakers once wore the *kabai*, a knee-length frock; later, shirts with knee-length trousers, a style still jokingly linked with bakers. Accounts were kept in pencil on a wall and paid monthly. The trade paid well, and bakers looked well-fed and prosperous.
slides.narration: The last stage explains the baker's place in village life. Bread is needed for every celebration, from marriage gifts of sweet bol, to engagement sandwiches, to Christmas cakes. Bakers once wore a knee-length frock called the kabai. They kept monthly accounts in pencil on a wall. And the trade paid well: bakers and their families never went hungry, and they looked it.

slides.heading: Bread for every occasion

rows: bread for the sandwiches her mother makes

visual.alt: Table of occasions and what the baker supplies: bol for marriage gifts, bread for engagement sandwiches, cakes and bolinhas for Christmas, bread-bangles for children, and loaves for every household.

slides.narration: This table shows why the baker matters so much. Marriage gifts need bol. A mother needs bread for the sandwiches at her daughter's engagement. Christmas and other festivals need cakes and bolinhas. Children want their bread-bangles, and every household buys loaves. Bread runs through Goan social and religious life, so a village without a baker would feel incomplete.

slides.narration: Check yourself. When the baker came, what did the children want most? Remember who bought the loaves.

slides.heading: Theme: tradition and change
slides.body_md: The piece is about a tradition that has outlived the rulers who began it.
columns:
**What has changed**

- Portuguese rule has ended
- the *kabai* has given way to shirts and knee-length trousers
- the elders' favourite loaves are a memory

**What survives**

- the furnaces and the bakers
- the sound of the bamboo staff in some villages
- bread at every celebration; the name *pader*
slides.narration: The main theme is tradition and change. Some things have changed: Portuguese rule is over, the baker's dress has changed, and the elders' favourite loaves are now a memory. But much survives: the furnaces, the bakers themselves, the sound of the bamboo staff in some places, and bread at every Goan celebration. A tradition can outlive the people who started it.

slides.heading: Tone: nostalgic and humorous (SOYL's own examples)
slides.body_md: Rodrigues writes with **nostalgia** (fond longing for the past) and **gentle humour**. These lines are SOYL's own, showing the same tones:
bullets: *Those summer evenings at my grandmother's house still smell of jasmine and frying pakoras.* — nostalgia
*We never did our homework before the ice-cream man had come and gone; priorities were priorities.* — gentle humour
*The old cinema is a mall now, but I can still hear the creak of its wooden seats.* — nostalgia with a sense of change
slides.narration: Rodrigues writes with nostalgia and gentle humour. Here are lines of our own showing the same tones. Those summer evenings at my grandmother's house still smell of jasmine and pakoras: that is nostalgia. We never did homework before the ice-cream man had come and gone: that is gentle humour. Now find similar moments in your textbook, such as the joke about brushing teeth.

slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and whether the reason really explains why every Goan village needs its baker.

slides.narration: Learn these words for this piece. A pader is a Goan baker, and a kabai was his old knee-length frock. Bol is a sweet bread for marriage gifts. Nostalgic means fondly longing for the past. Heralding means announcing. A rebuke is a scolding. Physique means body shape. And testimony means proof, like the baker's well-fed look proving his trade was profitable.

bullets: Older Goans miss the Portuguese loaves; the *pader* still bakes, often son after father.
Childhood: the baker came twice a day; children wanted bread-bangles, not loaves.
Bread for every occasion: *bol* (marriage gifts), sandwiches (engagements), cakes and *bolinhas* (Christmas).
The *kabai*; accounts on a wall, paid monthly; a profitable trade.
Tone: nostalgic and humorous. Read the piece in *First Flight*.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Older Goans miss the Portuguese loaves, but the pader still bakes. In the writer's childhood, the baker came twice a day and the children wanted bread-bangles. Bread marks every celebration. The baker wore the kabai, kept accounts on a wall, and prospered. The tone is nostalgic and humorous. Remember to read the piece in your textbook.

Facts often confused: the servants bought the loaves; bills were paid monthly, not daily.
Tone questions: nostalgic and humorous, with one detail for each.

Learn the Goan words exactly, because they are often tested. Remember that the servants bought the loaves, and that bills were paid monthly. And for tone questions, say nostalgic and humorous, and give one detail for each.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now we travel to Coorg, a hill district in Karnataka, through a piece by Lokesh Abrol. Please read it in your textbook, First Flight, before you continue. This lesson does not repeat the text. We will look at the land, the wildlife, the Kodavu people, the features of travel writing, and how to answer board questions.

slides.heading: The piece and the place

rows: Coorg (Kodagu), the smallest district of Karnataka, between Mysore and Mangalore
rolling hills; evergreen rainforest over about 30 per cent of the district; coffee and spices
heavy monsoon rain; best season September to March
the Kodavus: hospitable, brave, with a martial tradition

visual.alt: Table of facts about Part Two: Coorg by Lokesh Abrol, travel writing about Kodagu, the smallest district of Karnataka, between Mysore and Mangalore; hills, rainforest over about thirty per cent of the district, coffee and spices; heavy monsoon, best season September to March; the Kodavu people.

slides.narration: Coorg, also called Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka, lying between Mysore and the coastal city of Mangalore. It is a land of hills, evergreen rainforest, coffee and spices. The monsoon is very heavy, so the best time to visit is from September to March. The piece describes all this with open admiration, like a travel writer inviting us to come.

slides.heading: The piece in five parts
slides.body_md: A guided tour: place, seasons, people, river and wildlife, adventure. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of Coorg in five parts: where Coorg is; climate and seasons; the Kodavus; the Kaveri and its wildlife; adventure and sights.
visual.caption: Coorg in five parts (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The piece reads like a guided tour in five parts. First, where Coorg is. Second, its climate and seasons. Third, its people, the Kodavus. Fourth, the river Kaveri and its wildlife. And fifth, the adventures and sights waiting for visitors. Keep this map in mind as we go through each part.

slides.heading: Summary 1: land and seasons
slides.body_md: Abrol presents Coorg as a beautiful hill country. Evergreen rainforest covers about thirty per cent of the district. The monsoon rain is heavy enough to keep many visitors away, and the pleasant season runs from September to March, with only occasional showers. Coffee estates and old colonial bungalows stand among the trees.
slides.narration: The piece opens with the land. Coorg is described as a place of great natural beauty. Rainforest covers about a third of the district. The monsoon is heavy, so many visitors stay away then. From September to March the weather is pleasant, with only some showers. Coffee estates and old colonial bungalows sit among the trees.

slides.heading: Summary 2: the Kodavus
slides.body_md: The Kodavus are proud, independent people, possibly of Greek or Arab descent. Their homes are known for hospitality and for stories of brave sons and fathers. The Coorg Regiment is among the most decorated in the Indian Army; General Cariappa, the first Indian to head the Indian Army, was a Kodavu; and Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence.
slides.narration: Next come the people. The Kodavus are proud and independent, and two theories, Greek and Arab, are offered for their origin. They are famous for hospitality, and for courage. The Coorg Regiment is one of the Indian Army's most decorated, General Cariappa, the first Indian to head the army, was a Kodavu, and Kodavus may carry firearms without a licence.

slides.heading: Where did the Kodavus come from?

rows: soldiers of Alexander's army settled here when they could not return home
martial traditions; marriage and religious rites distinct from the Hindu mainstream
the *kuppia*, a long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt, resembles the Arab and Kurdish *kuffia*

visual.alt: Table of the two theories of Kodavu origin: Greek, from soldiers of Alexander's army, supported by martial traditions and distinct rites; and Arab, supported by the resemblance of the kuppia coat to the kuffia.
visual.caption: Two theories, neither proven.

slides.narration: There are two theories about the Kodavus' origin. The Greek theory says part of Alexander's army settled here when going home became impossible, and points to their martial traditions and distinct customs. The Arab theory points to their long black coat, the kuppia, which looks like the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds. Remember: these are theories, not proven facts.

slides.heading: Check: the Kodavu coat
slides.narration: Check yourself. The Kodavus wear a long black coat called the kuppia. What is it said to resemble, and which theory does that support?

slides.heading: Summary 3: the Kaveri and its wildlife
slides.body_md: The river Kaveri draws its water from Coorg's hills and forests. Its clear waters hold the mahaseer, a large freshwater fish. Kingfishers dive for fish, squirrels and langurs play in the trees, and elephants get a wash in the river from their mahouts. The forest is home to macaques and langurs, the Malabar squirrel, the shy slender loris, and countless birds and butterflies.
slides.narration: The third part is about the river and wildlife. The Kaveri gets its water from Coorg's hills and forests, and its clear pools hold a big fish called the mahaseer. Kingfishers dive, squirrels and langurs play, and elephants enjoy being bathed by their mahouts. The forest is full of birds, butterflies, monkeys and the shy slender loris.

slides.heading: Summary 4: adventure and sights
slides.body_md: Coorg offers plenty for adventurous visitors: mountain biking, rock climbing, rappelling, canoeing and river rafting, as well as walking trails for trekkers. The Brahmagiri hills give a view over the whole district; a rope bridge leads to the island of Nisargadhama; and visitors may meet Buddhist monks from Bylakuppe, India's largest Tibetan settlement.
slides.narration: Finally, adventure and sights. Coorg offers mountain biking, rock climbing, rappelling, canoeing, river rafting and trekking. A climb up the Brahmagiri hills gives a view over the whole district. A rope bridge leads to the island of Nisargadhama. And visitors may meet Buddhist monks from Bylakuppe, the largest Tibetan settlement in India.

slides.heading: Check: the monsoon in Coorg
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Read both statements about Coorg's weather carefully, and decide whether each is true.

slides.heading: Theme: a land and its people
slides.body_md: Coorg is shown as remarkable for both its nature and its people.
columns:
**The land**

- hills, rainforest, coffee and spices
- the Kaveri and the mahaseer
- elephants, langurs, kingfishers, the slender loris

**The people**

- the Kodavus, possibly of Greek or Arab descent
- famous hospitality and stories of valour
- the Coorg Regiment; General Cariappa
slides.narration: The main theme is that Coorg is special in two ways. The land is rich: hills, forest, coffee, a great river and wonderful wildlife. The people are just as remarkable: the Kodavus, with their mysterious origins, their hospitality and their proud military tradition. In long answers, cover both the land and the people, with details for each.

slides.heading: Style: features of travel writing
bullets: **Admiring description:** Coorg is presented as almost heavenly.
**Vivid detail:** colours, smells, sounds and creatures.
**Practical facts:** location, size, seasons, how much forest.
**History and legend:** the theories of Kodavu origin.
**An invitation:** adventure for the energetic, calm for the rest.
slides.narration: Coorg is a good example of travel writing. It describes the place with admiration, almost as a paradise. It uses vivid details of colours, smells and creatures. It gives practical facts like location and seasons. It mixes in history and legend. And it ends up as an invitation, offering adventure for the energetic and quiet beauty for everyone else.

slides.heading: Writing like a travel writer: SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: Travel writers combine **vivid description**, **practical facts** and **mild exaggeration**. These lines are SOYL's own, about an imaginary hill town:
bullets: *Morning mist pours down the valley like milk, and the tea stalls fill with the smell of ginger.* — vivid description with a simile
*The town lies four hours by road from the nearest airport; visit between October and February.* — practical facts
*Every bend in the road seems to reveal a view more beautiful than the last.* — mild exaggeration
slides.narration: Here are travel-writing lines of our own, about an imaginary hill town. Morning mist pours down the valley like milk: vivid description with a simile. The town lies four hours from the airport; visit between October and February: practical facts. Every bend reveals a view more beautiful than the last: mild exaggeration. Abrol uses all three. Find them in your textbook.

slides.narration: Check yourself. A school wants a trip with adventure sports, wildlife and a Tibetan settlement. Which place from the chapter suits it best?

slides.narration: Tea from Assam is a short story told in the third person. Rajvir, a boy from Delhi, travels with his classmate Pranjol to Pranjol's home in Upper Assam, where Pranjol's father, Mr Barua, manages a tea garden. The story mixes the boys' conversation with facts and legends about tea. The places to remember are Mariani junction and the Dhekiabari tea estate.

slides.heading: The story in five stages
slides.body_md: A journey that is also a lesson about tea. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

nodes.label: The first sight of the gardens

visual.alt: Flow of Tea from Assam: tea on the train; the first sight of the gardens; two legends and some history; met at Mariani; Dhekiabari and the second flush.
visual.caption: Tea from Assam in five stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves in five stages. The boys drink tea on the train. Rajvir sees the tea gardens for the first time. He tells Pranjol two legends and some history of tea. Pranjol's parents meet them at Mariani junction. And on the drive to Dhekiabari, Rajvir impresses Mr Barua with what he knows about the tea season.

slides.heading: Summary 1: the journey
slides.body_md: Rajvir and Pranjol, classmates in Delhi, travel by train to Pranjol's home in Upper Assam for the summer vacation. At a station they buy tea from a vendor, and Rajvir shares a fact: over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk around the world every day. Pranjol is absorbed in a detective novel. Soon Rajvir sees tea bushes stretching into the distance, shaded by tall trees, with pluckers at work and a factory's chimneys smoking.
slides.narration: The story begins on a train. Rajvir is going with his classmate Pranjol to spend the summer vacation on a tea estate in Assam. They buy tea at a station, and Rajvir says the world drinks over eighty crore cups every day. Pranjol keeps reading his detective novel. Then Rajvir sees tea gardens stretching into the distance, and he is thrilled.

slides.heading: Summary 2: legends and history of tea
slides.body_md: Pranjol explains that Assam has more tea plantations close together than anywhere in the world. Rajvir, who has read about tea, tells two legends of its discovery and adds some history.

rows: leaves from the fire under an emperor's pot fell into his boiling water and flavoured it
Bodhidharma cut off his eyelids to stay awake; ten tea plants grew from them
drunk in China around 2700 BC; *tea*, *chai* and *chini* come from Chinese
arrived in the sixteenth century, drunk at first as a medicine
more tea plantations close together than anywhere else in the world
May to July: the sprouting season that gives the best tea

visual.alt: Table of tea legends and facts from the story: the Chinese legend of leaves falling into an emperor's boiling water; the Indian legend of Bodhidharma's eyelids; tea first drunk in China around 2700 BC; reaching Europe in the sixteenth century as medicine; Assam's many plantations; and the second flush from May to July.

slides.narration: Pranjol tells Rajvir that Assam has more tea plantations than anywhere else in the world. Rajvir then shares what he has read. In a Chinese legend, leaves fell into an emperor's boiling water by accident. In an Indian legend, the monk Bodhidharma cut off his eyelids to stay awake, and tea plants grew from them. Tea reached Europe in the sixteenth century, as a medicine.

slides.heading: Summary 3: Dhekiabari and the second flush

**Read the chapter itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

*Glimpses of India* brings together three short pieces about three regions: **Part I, *A Baker from Goa*** by Lucio Rodrigues, a personal memoir; **Part II, *Coorg*** by Lokesh Abrol, a piece of travel writing; and **Part III, *Tea from Assam*** by Arup Kumar Datta, a short story mixing dialogue, facts and legends.

sections.heading: 2. Part I: A Baker from Goa (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**The past and the present.** Older Goans miss the Portuguese era and its bread. The rulers are gone, but the bakers remain: furnaces are still lit, the bamboo staff still announces the baker in some villages, and sons often carry on the trade. The baker is still called a *pader*.

**Childhood.** The baker came at least twice a day. Children ran to him for bread-bangles and sweet bread; servants bought the loaves. Pushed aside, the children climbed up to peep into the basket.

**Bread in Goan life.** *Bol* is essential to marriage gifts; mothers make sandwiches for a daughter's engagement; Christmas needs cakes and *bolinhas*. Every village needs its baker's furnace.

**Dress, accounts, prosperity.** Bakers once wore the *kabai*, a knee-length frock, and later shirts with knee-length trousers. Accounts were kept in pencil on a wall and paid monthly. The trade was profitable, and bakers looked well-fed.

**Tone:** nostalgic and gently humorous.

sections.heading: 3. Part II: Coorg (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**The land.** Coorg (Kodagu), the smallest district of Karnataka, lies between Mysore and Mangalore. Rainforest covers about thirty per cent of it; coffee and spices grow there. The monsoon is heavy; the best season is September to March.

**The people.** The Kodavus may be of Greek descent (from Alexander's soldiers) or Arab descent (their *kuppia* coat resembles the *kuffia*). They are known for hospitality and valour: the Coorg Regiment is among the Indian Army's most decorated, General Cariappa (the first Indian to head the army) was a Kodavu, and Kodavus may carry firearms without a licence.

**River and wildlife.** The Kaveri draws its water from Coorg; the mahaseer lives in it. Kingfishers, squirrels, langurs, elephants with their mahouts, macaques, Malabar squirrels and the slender loris appear.

**Adventure and sights.** Rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, mountain biking, trekking; the Brahmagiri hills; the rope bridge to Nisargadhama; Buddhist monks from Bylakuppe, India's largest Tibetan settlement.

**Tone:** admiring, descriptive travel writing.

sections.heading: 4. Part III: Tea from Assam (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**The journey.** Rajvir travels with his classmate Pranjol to Pranjol's home on a tea estate in Upper Assam. At a station they buy tea; Rajvir says over eighty crore cups are drunk worldwide every day. Pranjol reads a detective novel. Rajvir is thrilled by his first view of the tea gardens.

**Legends and history.** Pranjol says Assam has more plantations close together than anywhere else. Rajvir tells the Chinese legend (leaves from the fire fell into an emperor's boiling water) and the Indian legend (Bodhidharma cut off his eyelids to stay awake; ten tea plants grew from them). Tea was drunk in China around 2700 BC and reached Europe in the sixteenth century, first as medicine.

**Dhekiabari.** Pranjol's parents meet the boys at Mariani junction and drive to Dhekiabari, managed by Pranjol's father, Mr Barua. Pluckers pick new leaves; Rajvir identifies the second flush (May to July, the best tea). Mr Barua is impressed; Rajvir hopes to learn more.

**Tone:** light, informative, conversational.

1. Mixing up the Goan words: *pader* (baker), *kabai* (dress), *bol* (sweet bread), *bolinhas* (cookies).
2. Stating a Kodavu origin theory as fact.
3. Saying Pranjol tells the legends: Rajvir does.

Dhekiabari, first evening

What a day! From the train I saw tea bushes running on for miles, with tall trees shading them and a factory chimney smoking in the distance. Pranjol barely looked up from his detective novel. answer.model_answer_md: The three pieces take us to three very different corners of India. *A Baker from Goa* shows a coastal culture shaped by Portuguese rule, where bread marks every festival and the pader is a beloved figure; its tone is nostalgic and humorous. *Coorg* describes a hill district of Karnataka with rainforests, coffee and the river Kaveri, home to the proud Kodavus with their martial traditions; its tone is admiring, like a travelogue. *Tea from Assam* takes us to the vast tea gardens of the north-east through the eyes of a curious schoolboy, mixing legends and facts.
